Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Issue CategoryCriticalityStory Point
CVE-2025-55315: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2025-55315: .NET Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability
 Mandatory 1
File
eShopLegacyMVCSolution/eShopPorted/eShopPorted.csproj:7

Explanation

CVE-2025-55315. Severity: CRITICAL. Existing eShopPorted assets resolve Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core 2.2.0 through Microsoft.AspNetCore 2.2.0 -> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel -> Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core. GitHub lists <=2.3.0 as affected by HTTP request smuggling/security-feature bypass and 2.3.6 as patched. Deployment and request-processing prerequisites were not verified. Upgrade to a supported patched framework dependency set; compatibility of an isolated transitive override is unverified. Fresh dependency resolution failed because Microsoft.WebApplication.targets was unavailable; existing assets are not proof of deployed versions.
CVE-2024-0056: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient and System.Data.SqlClient vulnerable to SQL Data Provider Security Feature Bypass
 Mandatory 1
File
eShopLegacyMVCSolution/eShopPorted/eShopPorted.csproj:22

Explanation

CVE-2024-0056. Severity: HIGH. Existing eShopPorted assets resolve System.Data.SqlClient 4.6.1 through Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer 2.2.6, matching affected range <4.8.6. The advisory identifies SQL data-provider security-feature bypass. Connection-security and network-attack prerequisites were not demonstrated. Upgrade to 4.8.6 or a compatible supported successor. Fresh resolution failed; existing assets are not proof of deployed versions.

Data Storage & External Services

The applications configure different LocalDB database names, not a proven shared live database. Legacy defaults to database mode; the port defaults to an in-process mock. Images are local files. Legacy Application Insights collectors are configured, but no active instrumentation key is present in its configuration, so a functioning remote telemetry integration is not established. No message broker, cache server, gateway, or outbound business API integration was found in the scoped source. See data-architecture.md and configuration-inventory.md. [A4–A7]

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Both web applications implement the same catalog context independently; the utility is a library, not a third deployable service. All three are solution members; extra projects: none. [A1]
  • Controllers delegate directly to ICatalogService; implementations query their own DbContext rather than a separate repository layer. Mock services are singleton mutable lists, not caches. [A5], [A8]
  • The port is incomplete: its picture controller still derives from System.Web.Mvc.Controller, and binary export returns Ok(Stream) rather than the legacy streamed response. These are source-level compatibility caveats, not runtime-verified behavior. [A9]

Routing and compatibility caveats

  • CatalogController2 ends in Controller2, not the conventional Controller suffix; its MVC route attribute is not proof that MVC discovers it. It also calls legacy Json without AllowGet, so even discovery would not establish a working GET response. [P11]
  • The port's picture controller still uses System.Web.Mvc attributes/results and an empty picture-root string. Core MVC registration does not make these legacy attributes equivalent to Core routing/results. Catalog pages instead generate /Pics/{id}.png URLs for static images. [P10], [P6]
  • Ported brand/file Index actions have a controller route but no HttpGet restriction; ported brand-by-ID GET is absent. API parity with legacy is incomplete. [P9]
  • Export response parity is not established: legacy explicitly builds StreamContent, while the port returns an object result around a stream. [P8], [P9]

DTOs & Contracts

  • CatalogItem is a mutable service-level entity also used as MVC form input and view model; CatalogBrand is a mutable domain response. Their persistence fields belong in data-architecture.md. No gateway-level composition DTO exists. [P4], [P7]
  • Each FilesController defines its own mutable, [Serializable] nested BrandDTO for export. The similarly named DTOs are different CLR types in different assemblies/namespaces; a stable interoperable binary schema is not demonstrated. [P8], [P9]
  • PaginatedItemsViewModel carries paging/view results and is not immutable (TotalPages has a public setter). [P13]
  • Shared Serializing uses framework BinaryFormatter. No endpoint accepting uploaded serialized data or calling its deserializer was found; do not infer such an ingestion contract. Legacy brand APIs use Web API content negotiation; Core uses MVC object results with no custom serializer setup visible. [P8], [P9], [P14]
  • No scoped OpenAPI, protobuf, GraphQL schema, custom API versioning, or contract-testing artifact was found.

Communication Patterns

All controller-to-service and service-to-context operations are synchronous local calls. The utility is invoked directly in-process. No gateway, inter-application HTTP client, event broker, service discovery, load-balancer client, circuit breaker, retry policy, bulkhead, fallback-on-database-error, or explicit application timeout value was found. Mock selection is a startup option, not an automatic outage fallback. [P12], [P15]

Legacy startup configures its database initializer; ported startup registers the context only in database mode and does not apply migrations. Database availability can affect first data access; see configuration-inventory.md for startup details. No service-to-service boot ordering is declared.

Security posture: inspected controllers have no authentication/role/resource-ownership authorization attributes; legacy global filters contain only HandleError. Core startup does not register authentication/authorization middleware. Catalog POST forms have antiforgery protection, not identity authorization. Core development launch profiles offer HTTPS as well as HTTP and enable anonymous IIS access; no HTTPS redirection/TLS enforcement is present in Startup. Production IIS/proxy security policy is outside the scope and cannot be inferred. [P4], [P6], [P12], [P16], [P3]

Core Business Workflows

Users browse and maintain a merchandise catalog, classify products by brand/type, inspect product pictures, and export brand data. Stock thresholds are editable catalog metadata; no checkout, ordering, payment, automated replenishment, or shipment workflow is implemented in the inspected source.

Scope: D:\a\eShopModernizing\eShopModernizing\eShopLegacyMVCSolution only; both web applications and their shared library are solution members, and no extra scoped projects were found.

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships

CatalogBrandCatalog managementBrand reference dataClassifies multiple merchandise items
CatalogTypeCatalog managementProduct category/type reference dataClassifies multiple merchandise items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalog management and optional customized initializationCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeOwn configured database and local picture/setup files
eShopPortedAlternative catalog implementationSeparate copies of the same three entity conceptsOwn configured database if enabled; otherwise process-local demo data
eShopLegacy.UtilitiesTechnical export support; not an independent business serviceNoneFramework binary serializer

There is one conceptual catalog context, not separate brand, stock, and catalog microservices. Neither application calls the other or synchronizes its edits. [B3–B5]

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse catalog and view an item

  1. User enters the catalog page with optional paging inputs.
  2. The selected catalog service counts items and orders the requested page by item ID. Database implementations also load brand/type relationships; mock implementations compose references from predefined lists.
  3. The controller adds a presentation picture URI and renders the page. Item details lookups return a missing-input or not-found result where appropriate.
  4. Legacy picture delivery looks up the item and reads its configured local picture file. The ported catalog instead emits static picture URLs; its legacy-style picture controller is not an equivalent verified Core endpoint.

Sources: [B6–B8]. Paging input is not bounded by the controller; see rule R3 below.

Workflow 2: Create or edit merchandise

  1. User opens the create/edit form; the controller loads available brands and product types.
  2. User submits a catalog item and antiforgery token.
  3. MVC checks CatalogItem validation (R1), then the controller branches on ModelState validity.
  4. Valid creation invokes the selected service. Legacy database mode allocates an item ID from its HiLo generator, while ported database mode relies on database identity; mock mode assigns one above the current maximum.
  5. The database service saves the item, or mock mode mutates its in-process list. Success redirects to the catalog; invalid forms redisplay the item and refreshed dropdown choices.
  6. Editing marks the bound item modified in database mode; the mock replaces the matching list item.

Sources: [B6], [B7], [B9], [B10]. No inventory reservation or external notification is emitted.

Workflow 3: Confirm deletion, inspect brands, and export brands

  1. Item deletion has a read-only confirmation view followed by a token-protected form submission; the service removes the item and the controller redirects.
  2. Brand lookup returns the known brands or a not-found response for a missing legacy brand ID.
  3. The brand DELETE action in both apps is deliberately demo-only: it checks existence but never removes the brand.
  4. Export fetches brands, projects a BrandDTO list, and invokes the shared binary serializer. Legacy streams the serialized data; the port wraps the stream in an object result, so equivalent download behavior is not established.

Sources: [B6], [B7], [B11]. This is brand export only, not a product import/export round trip.

Workflow 4: Initialize a customized legacy catalog

  1. In database mode, startup installs the create-if-missing initializer.
  2. When initialization is triggered, it executes sequence scripts and seeds product types, brands, then items.
  3. If customization is enabled, it attempts to read setup CSV files; missing individual CSVs fall back to predefined data. CSV schema/type/brand resolution rules (R4) validate parsing.
  4. Types, brands and items are saved in separate stages.
  5. Customized pictures are provisioned by deleting current picture files and extracting the setup ZIP. Unlike missing CSV files, a missing/bad ZIP has no corresponding fallback branch.
  6. The port has model/migration seed declarations but no equivalent custom CSV/ZIP initialization call in Startup.

Sources: [B12–B14]. This process has filesystem effects and is not one atomic import transaction.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service composition, gateway aggregation, remote business API call, asynchronous business event, or distributed transaction was found. Catalog items and their brand/type labels are joined within the selected application's own DbContext or mock list, not across separately hosted services. The shared utility receives an in-process export projection and owns no business state. [B3], [B5], [B9–B11]

Database failure does not switch automatically to mock data. Mock selection is fixed by startup configuration and has process-local lifetime; it cannot provide coherent shared state across replicas. No circuit-breaker degradation or compensating business workflow is implemented. [B4], [B10], [B14]

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Catalog maintainer" participant Form as "Catalog controller" participant Rules as "CatalogItem validation" participant Service as "Selected catalog service" participant Store as "Catalog store" User->>Form: Open merchandise creation form Form->>Service: Load brand and type choices Service-->>Form: Reference data Form-->>User: Form and antiforgery token User->>Form: Submit merchandise details Form->>Rules: Validate bound catalog item alt Valid model Form->>Service: Create catalog item alt Database mode Service->>Store: Allocate ID and save item Store-->>Service: Save completed else Mock mode selected at startup Service->>Service: Allocate next list ID and append end Service-->>Form: Creation completed Form-->>User: Redirect to catalog listing else Invalid model Form->>Service: Reload brand and type choices Service-->>Form: Reference data Form-->>User: Redisplay form with validation errors end Note over Service,Store: No automatic fallback or compensation on storage failure

Business Rules & Decision Logic

RuleImplemented decision or constraintEvidence
R1 — CatalogItem validationName required. Price uses a numeric regular expression and inclusive range 0–1,000,000; its error text says positive, but the range permits zero. Available stock, restock threshold and maximum stock each have an independent inclusive range 0–10,000,000.Both entity files [B1]
R2 — Catalog relationships and defaultsNew items default picture filename to dummy.png. Brand/type choices are loaded for forms; required foreign-key relationships and ORM text lengths are enforced at persistence rather than fully mirrored by input annotations. No rule enforces stock below maximum or threshold ordering.[B1], [B6], [B7], [B15]
R3 — PaginationPage count is ceiling(total/pageSize); pageSize/pageIndex are accepted without explicit range validation. A zero page size can cause division by zero; there is no configured maximum page size.[B2], [B6], [B7]
R4 — CSV validationHeaders are normalized and checked; row/header widths must agree; type lookup must exist; price must parse using invariant culture; optional stock values parse as integers and reorder as Boolean. Empty brand/type labels are rejected. The brand-existence branch mistakenly checks the type dictionary with the brand name, so it is not a correct brand-validation guarantee.[B12], especially lines 192-224
R5 — Item identityLegacy allocates blocks of ten IDs from SQL sequence under a process lock; port uses SQL identity; mock creation chooses current max plus one and assumes a nonempty list.[B9], [B10], [B16]
R6 — Lifecycle semanticsItems are created, directly edited, or removed. OnReorder is editable metadata; no automatic stock/reorder state machine, uniqueness check, pricing promotion, or ordering lifecycle is present.[B1], [B9]
R7 — Demo brand deletionExisting brand returns success without mutation; absent brand returns not found.[B11]

Transactions: each database mutation uses one SaveChanges; no explicit cross-operation transaction, saga, or outbox is present. Legacy seed stages use multiple saves and file operations outside SQL atomicity. Errors: invalid forms are redisplayed, read actions handle missing IDs/items, but POST deletion does not explicitly guard a disappeared item; persistence/file errors have no business retry/compensation. The port configures a nondevelopment error handler referencing a Home error action, but no matching scoped Home controller was found. [B6], [B7], [B9], [B12], [B14]

Audit and authorization: controllers log reads and mutations, but no immutable business audit store/change history is implemented. Legacy request logging includes URL/user-agent context. Catalog writes require antiforgery tokens, but no business identity, role, or resource-ownership checks were found on these controllers; external hosting restrictions remain unknown. [B6], [B7], [B17]

Version & Compatibility Risks

The port targets net461, not .NET Core, despite ASP.NET Core 2.2 packages; ASP.NET Core/EF Core 2.2 and .NET Framework 4.6.1 are out-of-support technology lines. Legacy targets .NET Framework 4.7.2, whose support depends on its Windows host. Mixed legacy assembly HintPaths, packages.config, and PackageReference declarations require restore/build compatibility work; package declarations alone do not prove which assemblies load. This document does not assert CVEs or perform advisory resolution. [D1–D4]

Notable Observations

  • Legacy .csproj pins Autofac 6.1.0, while packages.config still lists 4.9.1; retain the discrepancy rather than treating the latter as authoritative. [D1], [D4]
  • Newtonsoft.Json differs across applications (12.0.1 versus 13.0.2); framework assemblies also appear as ordinary references and are not separate NuGet packages. [D1–D3]
  • No lockfiles, central package manifests, or test projects were found under the assessed folder. No transitive dependency tree was resolved.
  • All three projects are solution members; no extra scoped projects. Both apps reference the utility. Files above the scope were deliberately not inspected, so inherited repository-wide build settings are not established. [D5]

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

Three catalog entity concepts are independently implemented in each web project, using EF6 or EF Core with SQL Server; mock mode substitutes mutable process-local data. This assessment covers only D:\a\eShopModernizing\eShopModernizing\eShopLegacyMVCSolution, whose three projects are all solution members, with no extra scoped projects.

Entity Model

The diagram represents the common conceptual model, not cross-database relationships. Every entity is separately defined in each web project.

erDiagram CatalogBrand ||--o{ CatalogItem : "classifies brand" CatalogType ||--o{ CatalogItem : "classifies product type" CatalogBrand { int Id PK string Brand } CatalogType { int Id PK string Type } CatalogItem { int Id PK string Name string Description decimal Price string PictureFileName int CatalogTypeId FK int CatalogBrandId FK int AvailableStock int RestockThreshold int MaxStockThreshold bool OnReorder }
EntitySource / persisted fieldsPersistence characteristics
CatalogItemBoth Models\CatalogItem.cs:14-62 [E7]Diagram shows persisted scalar fields; PictureUri is computed for presentation and explicitly ignored by both mappings
CatalogBrandBoth Models\CatalogBrand.cs, legacy lines 8-11 [E8]Integer PK and required brand text, maximum 100 characters
CatalogTypeBoth Models\CatalogType.cs, legacy lines 8-11 [E8]Integer PK and required type text, maximum 100 characters

Item name is required and limited to 50 characters by both ORM mappings; price and picture filename are required. Description is optional. Integer foreign keys require a brand and type; navigation is unidirectional from item, with no inverse collections. Legacy explicitly disables database-generated item IDs, while the port's initial migration creates SQL identity columns. Ported foreign keys have cascade deletion and separate indexes; legacy required relationships rely on EF conventions rather than an explicit cascade override. No row-version/concurrency-token mapping was found. [E3], [E5], [E6]

Business input validation belongs in business-workflows.md; ORM length limits are not automatically equivalent to UI validation. Entity comments describe price precision, but neither mapping explicitly sets precision; the ported migration declares a decimal column without a type override. [E6], [E7]

Legacy initialization executes sequence SQL then saves types, brands, and items separately, and optionally extracts pictures from an archive. It is not a single atomic database-and-filesystem transaction. The ported migration seeds five brands, four types, and twelve items; mappings use HasData. No automatic migration call is visible in Startup/Program. [E4–E6], [E9]

Caching Strategy

No Redis, MemoryCache, distributed cache, explicit cache-aside/query cache, TTL, eviction policy, or second-level cache registration was found. The singleton CatalogServiceMock holds mutable demo data and composes brand/type references from predefined collections; it is an alternative source of truth for the process, not a cache of SQL data. Changes are lost on restart and not coordinated across instances. [E12]

Legacy sessions use InProc and record machine name/session start time. This is session state, not catalog caching, and no external session provider is configured. No ported session middleware registration was found. [E13], [E4]

Data Ownership Boundaries

These are parallel implementations of the same catalog context, not independently cooperating domain microservices. Default connections use different database names; no shared-database topology, cross-application SQL access, replication, or synchronization mechanism is established. Both serve reads and writes through one service/context model; no CQRS read model, event sourcing, or gateway aggregation exists in the inspected implementation. [E1], [E2], [E10]

The library owns no persistent data. Filesystem images and optional legacy setup CSV/ZIP assets are outside SQL transaction boundaries. Export DTOs are separate projections of catalog brand data, not another database-owning service. [E9], [E14]
